title: Future perfect continuous: emphasis on duration
question: By the time she retires, she _____ at that hospital for 35 years.
explanation: The future perfect continuous is 'will have been' + -ing and stresses duration up to a future point: 'by the time she retires'. 'Will be working' describes an action in progress, 'has been working' is present perfect continuous and 'had been working' is past perfect continuous.

title: Future perfect continuous form
question: By midnight, they _____ for twelve hours straight.
explanation: The future perfect continuous is 'will have been' + -ing and stresses duration up to a future point: 'by midnight'. 'Will be painting' describes an action in progress, 'have been painting' is present perfect continuous and 'would have been painting' is an unreal past.

title: Future perfect: completed quantity by a future point
question: By the end of the tour, the band _____ over 80 concerts.
explanation: The future perfect is 'will have' + past participle and describes a total completed by a future point: 'by the end of the tour'. 'Has played' and 'had played' look back from the present or from a past point, and 'would have played' is an unreal past.

title: Narrative past perfect: form
question: The streets were wet. It _____ heavily during the night.
explanation: The past perfect ('had' + past participle) explains the wet streets by an earlier event: it rained before the streets were seen wet. 'Has rained' is present perfect, 'would rain' is future-in-the-past and 'will have rained' is future perfect.

title: Past perfect continuous: form
question: His eyes were red because he _____ at the screen all day.
explanation: The past perfect continuous ('had been' + -ing) explains a past state (red eyes) by an activity that went on before it. 'Has been staring' is present perfect continuous, 'is staring' is present and 'will have been staring' is future perfect continuous.

title: Present perfect continuous: form
question: I _____ this book for three weeks and I'm only halfway through.
explanation: Present perfect continuous is 'have/has been' + -ing and links a past start to the present: 'for three weeks' and 'I'm only halfway through'. 'Read' is simple past, 'had been reading' is past perfect continuous and 'will have been reading' is future perfect continuous.

title: Past perfect continuous: interrupted duration
question: They _____ for an hour when the fire alarm went off.
explanation: The past perfect continuous ('had been' + -ing) shows an activity in progress before a later past event: the alarm. 'Have been waiting' is present perfect continuous, 'will have been waiting' is future perfect continuous and 'would wait' is a habitual or future-in-the-past form.

title: Future perfect vs future continuous: meaning
question: This time next year, I _____ my degree, so I'll be free to travel.
explanation: 'This time next year' with a finished degree needs the future perfect: 'will have + past participle'. 'Will be completing' is the future continuous and describes the degree as still in progress, which does not fit 'so I'll be free to travel'. 'Would complete' and 'had completed' point to the wrong time.

title: Tense in time clauses: no future after 'as soon as'
question: I'll call you as soon as I _____ at the hotel.
explanation: After 'as soon as', 'when', 'before', 'after' and 'until', English uses the present simple, not a future form. 'Will arrive', 'will be arriving' and 'would arrive' all put a future or conditional form in the time clause.

title: Future continuous: form
question: Please don't knock at noon -- the chef _____ lunch to the guests then.
explanation: The future continuous is 'will be' + -ing and shows an action in progress at a future moment: 'at noon'. 'Was serving' is past, 'has served' is present perfect and 'would serve' is a conditional form.

title: Future perfect passive: form
question: By Friday, the report _____ to every department.
explanation: Future perfect passive is 'will have been' + past participle: the report is the receiver of the action and is complete by Friday. 'Will have sent' is active and needs a person as subject, 'had been sent' is past perfect and 'would be sent' is conditional.

title: Past perfect: sequencing
question: By the time we reached the cinema, the film _____.
explanation: The earlier action takes the past perfect: 'had' + past participle. 'Has already started' is present perfect, 'would already start' is future-in-the-past and 'is already starting' is present continuous, so none of them fits a past reference point.

title: Nevertheless: which sentence uses it correctly?
question: Which sentence uses 'nevertheless' in a grammatically well-formed way?
correct: The results were disappointing; nevertheless, the team decided to continue.
wrong1: The results were disappointing, nevertheless, the team decided to continue.
wrong2: The results were disappointing nevertheless, the team decided to continue.
wrong3: The results were disappointing; nevertheless, but the team decided to continue.
explanation: 'Nevertheless' is a sentence adverb: it needs a full stop or semicolon before it and a comma after it. A comma alone creates a comma splice, no punctuation creates a run-on and adding 'but' duplicates the contrast.

title: Discourse marker at clause-final position
question: Which sentence places 'nonetheless' in a grammatically acceptable position?
correct: The evidence was weak. She pressed ahead with the claim nonetheless.
wrong1: The evidence was weak, nonetheless she pressed ahead with the claim.
wrong2: Nonetheless the evidence was weak, she pressed ahead with the claim.
wrong3: Nonetheless of the weak evidence, she pressed ahead with the claim.
explanation: 'Nonetheless' is a sentence adverb that can start or end a clause. It cannot join two clauses with only a comma, it is not a subordinating conjunction like 'although', and it is not followed by 'of' (that pattern belongs to 'despite' or 'notwithstanding').

title: Moreover: form and placement
question: Which sentence is grammatically well-formed?
correct: The restaurant was the best in town. Moreover, it was the cheapest.
wrong1: The restaurant was the best in town, moreover, it was the cheapest.
wrong2: The restaurant was the best in town moreover it was the cheapest.
wrong3: The restaurant was the best in town. Moreover that it was the cheapest.
explanation: 'Moreover' is a sentence adverb: it starts a new sentence (or follows a semicolon) and takes a comma. A comma alone is a comma splice, no punctuation is a run-on, and 'Moreover that' leaves an incomplete clause.

title: In contrast: linking parallel data
question: Which sentence is grammatically well-formed?
correct: Male participants improved by 40%. In contrast, female participants showed no change.
wrong1: Male participants improved by 40%, in contrast female participants showed no change.
wrong2: Male participants improved by 40% in contrast, female participants showed no change.
wrong3: Male participants improved by 40%. In contrast to, female participants showed no change.
explanation: 'In contrast' is a linking phrase that starts a new sentence (or follows a semicolon) and takes a comma. A comma alone is a comma splice, no punctuation is a run-on, and 'in contrast to' needs a noun phrase after it.

title: Consequently: form of the following clause
question: Funding was cut by 40%. Consequently, three research projects _____.
explanation: After 'consequently', a well-formed clause is required with subject-verb agreement: 'three projects were suspended'. 'Was suspended' does not agree with a plural subject, and 'suspended' and 'had suspended' are active forms that would need an object.

title: Indeed: intensifying the previous statement
question: The experiment confirmed our hypothesis. Indeed, the effect _____ even stronger than predicted.
explanation: 'Indeed' must be followed by a well-formed clause. 'The effect was' takes a singular verb; '*were', '*been', and '*being' are all ungrammatical as the main verb of this clause.

title: Collocation: make + mistake
question: She apologised because she had _____ a serious mistake in the report.
explanation: 'Make a mistake' is the fixed collocation. 'Do', 'take' and 'give' are real verbs but are not used with 'mistake'.

title: Collocation: take + responsibility
question: Someone has to _____ responsibility for the failure.
explanation: 'Take responsibility' is the fixed collocation. 'Make', 'do' and 'bring' are real verbs but are not used with 'responsibility' in this sense.

title: Collocation: do + damage
question: The storm _____ considerable damage to the coastline.
explanation: 'Do damage' is the standard collocation. 'Make', 'give' and 'take' are real verbs but are not used with 'damage' in this sense.

title: Collocation: make + profit
question: The company _____ a profit for the first time in years.
explanation: 'Make a profit' is the fixed collocation. 'Do', 'give' and 'have' are real verbs but are not used with 'profit' in this sense.

title: Collocation: pay + attention
question: Please _____ close attention to the safety instructions.
explanation: 'Pay attention' is the fixed collocation. 'Make', 'do' and 'take' are real verbs but are not used with 'attention' in this sense.

title: Word form: great + achievement
question: Winning the scholarship was a _____ achievement for her.
explanation: An adjective is needed before the noun: 'a great achievement'. 'Greatly' is an adverb, 'greatness' is a noun and 'greatest' would need 'the'.

title: Word form: large + amount
question: The project required a _____ amount of funding.
explanation: An adjective is needed before 'amount': 'a large amount'. 'Largely' is an adverb, 'largeness' is a noun and 'many' is used with countable plurals, not with 'amount'.

title: Collocation: heavy + smoker
question: Her doctor warned her that being a _____ smoker would shorten her life.
explanation: 'Heavy smoker' is a fixed collocation for someone who smokes a lot. 'Strong', 'hard' and 'deep' are real adjectives but are not used with 'smoker'.

title: Collocation: make + progress
question: The patient has _____ remarkable progress since the surgery.
explanation: 'Has made progress' is the fixed collocation and takes a past participle after 'has'. 'Done', 'taken' and 'got' are real participles but are not used with 'progress'.

title: Lay vs lie: present participle of transitive 'lay'
question: The workers spent the morning _____ new carpet throughout the office.
explanation: The present participle of transitive 'lay' (to put down) is 'laying', and it takes an object (carpet). 'Lying' is the participle of intransitive 'lie' (to recline), and 'laid' and 'lain' are past forms that cannot follow 'spent the morning'.

title: Lay vs lie: past of intransitive 'lie'
question: She felt dizzy, so she _____ down on the sofa for an hour.
explanation: The past tense of intransitive 'lie' (to recline) is 'lay'. 'Laid' is the past of transitive 'lay', 'lain' is a past participle that needs 'had' and 'lied' is the past of 'lie' meaning to tell an untruth.

title: Lay vs lie: past participle of 'lie'
question: He had _____ in bed all morning before anyone found him.
explanation: The past participle of intransitive 'lie' (to recline) is 'lain'. 'Had lay' is ungrammatical because a past tense cannot follow 'had', 'laid' is the participle of transitive 'lay' and 'lied' means told an untruth.

title: Lay vs lie: past of transitive 'lay'
question: She _____ the baby gently in the crib and tiptoed out.
explanation: 'Laid' is the past tense of transitive 'lay' (to put down), and it takes an object (the baby). 'Lay' is the base form (or the past of 'lie'), 'lain' is a participle that needs 'had' and 'lied' means told an untruth.

title: Lay vs lie: present participle of 'lie'
question: The cat has been _____ on my laptop all afternoon.
explanation: The present participle of intransitive 'lie' (to recline) is 'lying'. 'Laying' is the participle of transitive 'lay' and needs an object, 'lain' is a past participle that cannot follow 'been' here and 'lied' means told an untruth.

title: Affect vs effect: verb
question: Rising interest rates will _____ thousands of small businesses.
explanation: 'Affect' is the verb meaning to influence. 'Effect' as a verb means to bring about, so it does not fit here. 'Affirm' means to state firmly and 'adopt' means to take on.

title: Effect in a fixed phrase: take effect
question: The medicine takes _____ within twenty minutes.
explanation: 'Take effect' is the fixed phrase meaning to start working. 'Affect' is normally a verb, 'affection' means fondness and 'effort' means hard work.

title: Affect as a noun: form
question: The patient displayed a flat _____, showing no emotional response.
explanation: In psychology, 'affect' is the noun for the outward display of emotion, so a 'flat affect' shows no emotional response. 'Effect' means result, 'affection' means fondness and 'affectation' means pretended behaviour.

title: Effects: plural noun subject
question: The _____ of sleep deprivation on memory are well documented.
explanation: A plural subject is required to agree with 'are', and the noun meaning 'results' is 'effects'. 'Effect' and 'affect' are singular, and 'affects' is normally a verb form.

title: Fewer vs less: countable plural
question: Our team made _____ mistakes this season than last.
explanation: 'Fewer' is used with countable plural nouns in comparisons. 'Fewest' is a superlative and needs 'the', and 'less of' and 'fewer of' need a determiner after 'of'.

title: Less with distance
question: The airport is _____ than ten miles from here.
explanation: 'Less' is used with distances, even though miles can be counted. 'Lesser' means smaller in importance, 'least' is a superlative and 'smaller' describes size, not distance.

title: Less with sums of money
question: The repair cost _____ than £500.
explanation: A total sum of money takes 'less'. 'Lesser' means smaller in importance, 'least' is a superlative and 'lower' does not fit after 'cost' with 'than £500'.

title: Fewer with countable people
question: _____ than fifty delegates attended the second day of the conference.
explanation: A comparative with countable plural nouns uses 'fewer'. 'Fewest' and 'least' are superlatives, and 'lesser' means smaller in importance, not in number.

title: Lend: direction and form
question: My brother _____ me his bike every summer, so I don't need to buy one.
explanation: 'Lend' means to give something temporarily, and the third-person present needs '-s'. 'Borrows' reverses the direction, 'owes' means to have a debt and 'lent' is a past form that does not fit the present time frame.

title: Borrow: form after modal
question: Students can _____ up to five books from the library at a time.
explanation: 'Borrow' means to take something temporarily from someone. 'Lend' describes the library's action, 'owe' means to have a debt and 'lease' means to rent property under a contract.

title: Owe: present tense form
question: You paid for my lunch, so now I _____ you £15.
explanation: 'Owe' means to have a debt to someone. 'Lend' and 'borrow' describe temporary transfers and do not mean having a debt, and 'own' means to possess.

title: Lend: past tense (irregular)
question: She _____ him her car last weekend.
explanation: The past of 'lend' is 'lent'. 'Lend' and 'lends' are present forms that do not fit 'last weekend', and 'borrowed' reverses the direction of the action.

title: Reported speech: pronoun + past perfect form
question: She told me she _____ the email before the meeting started.
explanation: In reported speech about an earlier event, use the past perfect: 'had' + past participle. 'Has sent' does not backshift, and 'will send' and 'is sending' are present or future forms that do not fit 'before the meeting started'.

title: Third conditional: form of the if-clause
question: If they _____ earlier, they would have caught the train.
explanation: The third conditional if-clause is 'had' + past participle. 'Have left' lacks 'had', 'were leaving' is past continuous and 'would leave' does not belong in an if-clause.

title: Mixed conditional: past condition, present result
question: If she _____ the contract carefully last year, she would not be in legal trouble now.
explanation: The past condition in a mixed conditional takes the past perfect: 'had' + past participle. 'Has read' is present perfect, 'would read' does not belong in an if-clause and 'were reading' is past continuous.

title: Discourse: that said
question: The hotel was overpriced. _____, the location was unbeatable.
explanation: 'That said' is a fixed discourse marker that introduces a contrasting point. 'Moreover' adds a point, 'consequently' introduces a result and 'similarly' introduces a comparison.

title: Discourse: thereby + participle
question: She moved production in-house, _____ cutting costs by 20%.
explanation: 'Thereby' means 'by that means' and attaches directly to a present participle ('cutting'). 'Nevertheless' signals contrast, 'otherwise' signals an alternative condition and 'whereas' introduces a contrast between two clauses.

title: Collocation: do + justice
question: The photograph doesn't _____ justice to the actual landscape.
explanation: 'Do justice to something' means to represent it fairly or fully, and after 'doesn't' the base form 'do' is required. 'Make' and 'give' are real verbs but do not form this phrase, and 'serve justice' means something different.
